extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral philosophy; scholars studying Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes Aristotle's evaluative criteria and conceptual distinctions about demonstrative knowledge, first principles, and moral character (self-control, imperfect self-control/akrasia, brutality, endurance, softness) from Nicomachean Ethics (Books VII and preceding chapter on demonstration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for demonstrative knowledge (premises)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Knowledge produced by demonstrative reasoning must be drawn from premisses true and first, and incapable of syllogistic proof, and better known, and prior in order of time, and causes of the conclusion.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle elaborates that demonstrative syllogisms must have premises that are (a) true, (b) first/indemonstrable, (c) incapable of syllogistic proof, (d) better known than the conclusion, (e) prior in time or nature, and (f) causes of the conclusion. A syllogism lacking such premises is not a demonstration and does not produce knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning and role of 'first', 'thesis', and 'axiom'
rubrics_metrics.description: “By first I mean principles akin to the conclusion... the principle or first step in demonstration is a proposition incapable of syllogistic proof... I call that a thesis which you cannot demonstrate, and which is unnecessary with a view to learning something else. That which is necessary in order to learn something else is an Axiom.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes three statuses of fundamental propositions: 'first' (indemonstrable principles closely related to the conclusion), 'thesis' (cannot be demonstrated and unnecessary for learning other things), and 'axiom' (necessary for learning other things). Principles should be 'akin to the conclusion' so that they function as proper causes in demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstration vs mere syllogism
rubrics_metrics.description: “Syllogism, of course there may be without such premisses, but it will not be demonstration because it will not produce knowledge.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only syllogisms built from the specified kinds of first principles count as demonstrations that produce knowledge; formal syllogistic proofs from non-first or non-causal premises do not yield demonstrative knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistemic firmness and infallibility for demonstrative knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The person who possesses demonstrative Knowledge must “believe nothing more firmly than the contradictories of those principles out of which the contrary fallacy may be constructed: since he who knows, is to be simply and absolutely infallible.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle requires a robustness of belief in principles for genuine knowledge: one must not hold contrary beliefs that would allow construction of a fallacy; the knower should be free of such contradictions (idealized infallibility in practice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of moral defects to be avoided
rubrics_metrics.description: “Of what is to be avoided in respect of moral character there are three forms; Vice, Imperfect Self-Control, and Brutishness.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are presented as distinct species of moral failure with different natures and remedies. Their contraries are respectively Virtue, Self-Control, and (for brutishness) a superhuman/heroic godlike virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core distinctions: Self-Control vs Imperfect Self-Control vs Perfected Self-Mastery
rubrics_metrics.description: Common statements enumerated: I. Self-Control and Endurance are good/praiseworthy while Imperfect Self-Control and Softness are blameworthy. II. The man of Self-Control is identical with the man apt to abide by his resolution; the man of Imperfect Self-Control is apt to depart from his resolution. III. The man of Imperfect Self-Control does things at the instigation of his passions, knowing them to be wrong; the man of Self-Control, knowing his lusts to be wrong, refuses by the influence of reason. IV. The man of Perfected Self-Mastery unites Self-Control and Endurance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle uses these points to delineate moral types: Self-Control (enkrateia) implies adherence to one's resolutions by reason; Imperfect Self-Control (akrasia) implies yielding to passions despite knowing better; Perfected Self-Mastery is an ideal mean uniting mastery and endurance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Socrates' view and Aristotle's response on akrasia (knowledge and action)
rubrics_metrics.description: Socrates argued that if one truly knows what is best one cannot act against it (i.e., akrasia is impossible). Aristotle replies that this conflicts with plain facts and analyzes forms of ignorance or failure: the person may 'have' knowledge but not exercise it, or possess only opinion rather than knowledge, or be under the sway of passions that impair the practical use of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle distinguishes senses of 'knowing' (having knowledge vs exercising it), points out that passions can put one in states analogous to sleep/drunkenness/madness, and locates akrasia in failures of practical application (e.g., using universal premises but failing to apply particulars in practical syllogisms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical syllogism structure and how desire subverts action
rubrics_metrics.description: All action may be analysed into a syllogism with a universal maxim and a particular premiss cognizable by sense; if the particular is absent or not 'known' (only stated), desire can lead to the wrong minor premise winning out and the agent acting contrary to the universal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle explains akrasia mechanistically: the universal maxim may be present but the sensitive, particular premiss (the minor) is misperceived or unexercised under passion, so the desire-driven particular yields an action incompatible with reasoned conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Object-matter limitation of Self-Control and Imperfect Self-Control
rubrics_metrics.description: “The object-matter of Imperfect Self-Control and Self-Control is restricted to the same as that of utter absence of Self-Control and that of Perfected Self-Mastery... things which produce pleasure are either necessary, or objects of choice in themselves but yet admitting of excess... those who are excessive in their liking for such things contrary to the principle of Right Reason... is termed 'a man of Imperfect Self-Control'.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle limits the proper application of the terms enkrateia/akrasia to bodily pleasures and pains (touch and taste, basic appetites). For pursuits like honor, wealth, etc., the label 'imperfect self-control' is used only with a qualification (e.g., 'in respect of money'). Thus the taxonomy focuses on bodily appetites as the primary object-matter for akratic failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Softness/Luxury and Endurance; relation to Self-Control
rubrics_metrics.description: Softness and Luxury are the counterparts of Endurance and Self-Control: Endurance consists in continued resistance, Self-Control in actual mastery. The man who yields to temptations that common people can resist is Soft; the man who resists continuously is Enduring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle differentiates types of failure and excellence regarding pleasures and pains: softness = failure to withstand common trials; endurance = sustained resistance; self-control = immediate mastery. Self-control is regarded as more choice-worthy than mere endurance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of Imperfect Self-Control: Precipitancy and Weakness
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two forms: Precipitancy (those led by passion because they have not formed resolutions) and Weakness (those who have resolutions but do not abide by them because of passion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precipitancy is typical of quick or melancholic temperaments (act before reason catches up); Weakness is failure to adhere to an existing resolution. Some can resist by prearming their resolution against temptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of blameworthiness depends on object-matter and motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Akrasia in respect of lusts is more disgraceful than that in respect of anger because lust yields to pleasure (insolence yields pleasure) while anger acts with pain and in some sense 'listens to reason'. Also acts done from little or no desire can be judged worse than those from strong desire; utterly void of self-control (no remorse) is worse than imperfect self-control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle uses considerations like naturalness of the appetite, whether the action involves pleasure or pain, insidiousness, and the commonness of resistance among people to assess moral culpability. He gives literary and folkloric examples (Homer, Niobe, Philoctetes) to illustrate comparative disgrace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brutishness and morbid inclinations are distinct from Vice
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain inclinations (e.g., cannibalism; eating foetuses; unusual tastes caused by disease or custom) are Brutish or Morbid and not 'Vice' in the proper sense; when nature or disease is the cause, mastery or yielding is not properly called Self-Control or Imperfect Self-Control simply but only metaphorically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle separates these states from moral vice because they lack the proper rational deliberative structure; examples include pathological or culturally conditioned appetites. Such states may be described with qualifiers (e.g., 'brutish' or 'morbid') rather than labeled as ordinary moral failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curability and moral prognosis: incurable vice vs curable akrasia
rubrics_metrics.description: The man utterly void of Self-Control is incurable (lacks remorse); Imperfect Self-Control is like an acute disorder and may be curable, being 'almost made up of remorse'. Vice (deep depravity) resembles chronic disease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle uses medical analogies: some moral states are chronic and intractable (utter lack of self-control, deep vice), while others (imperfect self-control) admit remedy and improvement through education or correction.
